title.value: Performance reserves in brain-imaging-based phenotype prediction
title.justification: The paper title is clearly mentioned at the beginning and throughout the article.
title.quote: Performance reserves in brain-imaging-based phenotype prediction

analysis.description: This study investigates the impact of sample size on the prediction of cognitive and mental health phenotypes from brain imaging using machine learning. It analyzes how increasing sample sizes and integrating multiple imaging modalities can improve prediction accuracy. The paper highlights the challenges in achieving practical utility of these predictions despite significant performance reserves indicated by learning curves.

type.justification: The paper involves systematic evaluation and analysis of learning curves using empirical data from the UK Biobank and other datasets to draw conclusions about the prediction accuracy and sample size requirements.
type.quote: Our analysis shows a 3- to 9-fold improvement in prediction performance when sample size increases from 1,000 to 1 M participants.

name.justification: The paper discusses machine learning models and their application to neuroimaging data for phenotype prediction, focusing on how different imaging modalities and sample sizes affect prediction accuracy.
name.quote: This study examines the impact of sample size on predicting cognitive and mental health phenotypes from brain imaging via machine learning.

name.justification: The paper aims to address the feasibility of using neuroimaging data for precise, single-subject predictions relevant to precision medicine.
name.quote: The two questions of sample size and exploitable predictive information are closely related... this would provide estimates of the necessary sample size to reach a certain accuracy level as well as the highest achievable accuracy for a target phenotype given infinite samples

name.justification: The paper applies and validates theoretical concepts from statistical learning theory, particularly learning curve extrapolation and power-law scaling.
name.quote: Theoretical results from statistical learning theory state that the prediction accuracy typically scales as a power-law function of the sample size.

name.justification: The RBF-kernelized ridge regression model is specifically named and compared against linear models within the paper.
name.quote: Only in sex and age predictions based on DWI with large sample sizes above 16,000 did nonlinear models appear to marginally outperform their linear counterparts.

is_contributed.justification: The model is standard and known in the field, and not introduced in this paper as a new model.
is_contributed.quote: Only in sex and age predictions... did nonlinear models appear to marginally outperform their linear counterparts (Figure 5A.1).

is_executed.justification: The model was executed as part of the experiments for this study to compare its performance with linear models.
is_executed.quote: We replicated these analyses for age, sex, fluid intelligence, and depression and on up to 32,000 training samples, comparing linear ridge regression with its nonlinear counterpart, RBF-kernelized ridge regression.

is_compared.justification: The model’s performance is directly compared to that of linear models in the study, showing the extent of its prediction ability.
is_compared.quote: In recent work... we observed that linear and more expressive nonlinear machine learning models did not show relevant differences in performance for sex and age prediction.

referenced_paper_title.value: Learning Curves in Classification with Microarray Data
referenced_paper_title.justification: The model’s citation ties back to the broader body of knowledge on learning curves and empirical power-law scaling.
referenced_paper_title.quote: Theoretical results from statistical learning theory state that the prediction accuracy typically scales as a power-law function of the sample size. ^{29–32} Empirically, power-law scaling of learning curves has been shown for models ranging from linear estimators to deep neural networks. ^{33,34}...

name.justification: UK Biobank is the primary dataset analyzed in the study and provides comprehensive neuroimaging and phenotype data.
name.quote: We based our analyses on the UK Biobank brain imaging dataset, which is the largest uniformly acquired brain imaging dataset available to date (46,197 participants, June 2021 release).
